Upcycling Agro-Food Industrial Biomass Waste into Functional 
Activated Carbon for Selective CO
2 
Capture and Supercapacitor 
Applications 
Fahmi Anwar, Anish Mathai Varghese, Suresh Kuppireddy,* Nahla Alamoodi, and 
Georgios N. Karanikolos* 
ACCESS
|

ABSTRACT: Activated carbon (AC) materials were developed via a single-step method from three different biowaste sources and tailored 
for application in carbon dioxide (CO
2
) capture and electrochemical energy storage, combining the concept of biowaste valorisation with 
sustainable environmental and energy applications. This work investigated the use of three underexplored agro-food waste streams as 
precursors, namely flour mill waste (BW1), old corn waste (BW2), and feed waste (BW3), and performed a systematic comparison of their 
conversion under the same activation conditions, as well as characteristics and performance. The developed AC materials demonstrated 
properties such as high graphitization, favorable pore-structure configuration and surface area, and favorable surface characteristics. CO
2 
adsorption experiments at 298 K showed a capacity of 2.55 mmol/g at 1 bar with stability over multiple cycles for AC2, as well as high CO
2
/ 
N
2 
selectivity, reaching 48 at 1 bar (ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST)) for a 15:85 v/v CO
2
/N
2 
mixture for AC1, suggesting a high 
selective affinity for CO
2 
capture at ambient conditions. Furthermore, electrochemical experiments revealed stable performance as electric 
double-layer capacitors as a result of low solution and charge-transfer resistance, demonstrating capacitive performance in the order of 250 F/g 
at a scan rate of 5 mV/s for AC3, which was tested at different increasing scan rates and determined to retain a capacitance value higher than 
90 F/g at a high scan rate of 100 mV/s. Galvanostatic charge−discharge (GCD) investigations revealed virtually symmetric charge−discharge 
curves with an acceptable rate capability for a symmetric AC3 full cell, retaining ∼70% of initial capacitance despite a 4-fold increase in current 
density, and preserving ∼78% of initial capacitance after 1000 cycles. These results reveal the potential of agro-industrial waste streams- 
derived AC materials for selective carbon capture and electrochemical energy storage, enabling them a simple, potentially scalable, and 
sustainable material platform for such applications. The key contribution is the processing of three previously underutilized agro-food 
industrial biomass wastes into functional AC materials for energy storage and CO
2 
capture via a single-step KOH activation approach, 
allowing for direct comparison and correlation of precursor chemistry. Furthermore, this provides a solid basis for future precursor-specific 
tuning of KOH loading, activation temperature and time, pore structure, and surface functioning to optimize properties and performance. 
KEYWORDS: biomass waste and upcycling, activated carbon and functional materials, CO
2 
capture and adsorption, adsorbents, super-
capacitor and energy storage 
1. INTRODUCTION 
Activated carbon (AC) from biowaste is a sustainable and cost- 
effective approach to develop porous materials with tunable 
pore structure, high surface area and surface chemistry.
1 
It bears 
potential for environmental protection and energy storage re-
lated applications, including advanced carbon capture and 
electrochemical supercapacitor systems, because of the avail-
ability of various source materials and the highly favorable 
physicochemical properties of the resulting products.
2,3 
Glob-
ally, agricultural waste generation exceeds 1 billion tonnes

annually, much of which is disposed of through landfilling or 
open burning, contributing to environmental pollution.
4 
Con-
verting these residues into AC provides a value-added waste 
utilization pathway while lowering disposal costs. Furthermore, 
biomass-derived AC can be produced at costs as low as 
1.34 USD/kg, highlighting its potential as a sustainable and 
economically viable alternative to conventional carbon mate-
rials.
5 
The potential of biowaste-derived AC to function as an 
effective adsorbent for carbon dioxide (CO
2
) capture while also 
demonstrating high electrochemical performance for super-
capacitor applications provides new opportunities to address 
two pressing global challenges: CO
2 
accumulation and energy 
crisis.
6 
This concept also establishes structure−property cor-
relations that can be used to rationally design next-generation 
CO
2 
capture based on electrochemically motivated systems. 
CO
2 
capture has emerged as a vital strategy for minimizing 
the impact of climate change.
5,6 
The buildup and rising con-
centration of CO
2 
in the atmosphere leads to global warming, 
making it vital to develop effective technologies for capturing 
and storing greenhouse gases.
7−10 
Among the various tech-
nologies, selective capture by solid adsorbent systems is a po-
tential technique for CO
2 
capture due to its affordability, ease of 
operation in ambient conditions, and low energy 
requirements.
11,12 
AC, with a high surface area, and adjustable 
pore structure and surface chemistry, has been demonstrated to 
be a suitable adsorbent for CO
2 
capture.
13 
In this context, 
attempts have also been made to develop AC adsorbents from 
various biomass sources. For instance, an AC produced from 
lotus seeds had an adsorption capacity of 3.1 mmol/g at 25 °C 
and 1 bar due to high specific surface area of up to 2230 m
2
/g as 
well as tunable ultra-microporosity.
14 
Pine cone-derived carbon 
showed a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 1.91 mmol/g under 
ambient conditions, owing to well-defined microporous struc-
ture and the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups.
15 
Furthermore, tea seed shells were used to produce AC, which 
was then modified with melamine to add more nitrogen, re-
sulting in a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 3.15 mmol/g at 25 °C 
and 1 bar due to the presence of a microporous structure with 
nitrogen functional groups.
16 
At 1 bar, the CO
2 
uptake of olive 
stone-derived AC, which was produced using an eco-friendly 
bioorganic method and had a high surface area and ultra-
microporous structure, was 4.33 mmol/g (at 30 °C).
1 
Likewise, 
biochar-derived AC produced via KOH activation demonstrated 
steady CO
2 
breakthrough performance, revealing the impor-
tance of activation and micropore framework tailoring for gas 
separation at practical conditions.
17 
Amazonian fruit waste- 
derived AC with well developed narrow microporosity 
showed 4.81 mmol/g of CO
2 
adsorption at 1 bar and 25 °C.
18 
Building on this concept, multisubstrate agricultural waste- 
based AC prepared from a blend of peanut shells, coffee 
husks, corn cobs, and banana peels demonstrated an adsorption 
capacity of 2.01 mmol/g (8.86 wt %) and a CO
2 
removal ef-
ficiency of up to 96.2%.
19 
Recent investigations have shown that heteroatom-doped 
biomass-derived carbons, such as N,S co-doped and boron- 
doped systems, can further enhance CO
2 
uptake and selectivity 
by introducing additional adsorption sites and modulating the 
electronic characteristics of the carbon framework.
20,21 
Col-
lectively, these studies demonstrate that high surface area, 
abundant ultra-microporosity, and heteroatom functionalities 
are key elements influencing CO
2 
adsorption performance, yet 
the adsorption behavior strongly depends on precursor type and 
synthesis method. Desert biomass wastes have recently been 
identified as interesting precursors for high-performance CO
2 
adsorbents.
22 
Asmaly et al.
23 
synthesized AC from Balanites 
aegyptiaca seed shells and reported a large surface area exceeding 
3000 m
2
/g, resulting in a CO
2 
uptake of 5.2 mmol/g at 25 °C. 
Similarly, AC produced from desert date seed husk via KOH 
activation achieved a surface area of ∼2000 m
2
/g and a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 3 mmol/g at 25 °C, together with a CO
2
/ 
N
2 
selectivity of 2.65, highlighting the effectiveness of desert 
agricultural waste valorization for carbon capture applications.
24 
Recent reviews have highlighted that biomass- and waste- 
derived AC with abundant ultra-microporosity and tailored 
surface functionalities can achieve CO
2 
capacities exceeding 
6−9 mmol/g under near-ambient conditions.
25 
This superior 
adsorption performance is primarily governed by the pore size 
distribution and surface chemistry of the AC. In particular, 
narrow micropores and ultra-micropores are highly effective for 
CO
2 
capture because their dimensions closely match the kinetic 
diameter of CO
2 
(0.33 nm), resulting in enhanced adsorba-
te−adsorbent interactions through overlapping adsorption 
potentials.
26 
Thus, at 25 °C and 1 bar, AC enriched with ultra- 
micropores have shown CO
2 
adsorption capacities exceeding 
4−6 mmol/g.
27,28 
On the other hand, supercapacitors, also known as electro-
chemical capacitors, are energy storage devices with high power 
density, cyclic performance, and fast charge−discharge rates, 
making them suitable options for applications requiring rapid 
energy delivery, such as electric vehicles, portable electronics, 
and renewable energy systems.
29,30 
Yet, developing cost- 
effective, high-performance supercapacitors that can meet ris-
ing energy demands remains a challenge. AC is one of the most 
popular materials for supercapacitor electrodes due to its large 
surface area, electrical conductivity, and favorable electro-
chemical characteristics.
31 
Based on this, using biomass as a 
precursor, efforts have been made to generate AC exhibiting 
improved supercapacitor performance while reducing the en-
vironmental impact of conventional AC sources.
32,33 
For ex-
ample, AC based on sorghum pith activated with NaOH was 
used to produce electrodes with a high specific capacitance of 
320.6 F/g.
34 
Titania-supported AC produced from Oleander 
seeds with the synergistic effects of electric double-layer ca-
pacitance of carbon and pseudocapacitive properties of titania, 
resulted in a specific capacitance of 214 F/g at 1 A/g with good 
cyclic stability.
35 
A nitrogen self-doped AC was synthesized 
from shrimp shell waste using CaCO
3 
as a self-template, ex-
hibiting a high specific capacitance of 225 F/g, and energy and 
power densities of 11.23 Wh/kg and 248.8 W/kg, respectively.
36 
Shea butter waste was used to produce a hierarchical porous 
carbon through a two-stage activation method that produced an 
optimized material with high specific capacitance of 286.6 F/g, 
with a focus on practical applications related to powering LED 
bulbs.
37 
Nitrogen-doped carbon derived from tea seed shells via 
melamine modification showed a specific capacitance of 141 F/g 
at 0.5 A/g, owing to the microporous structure and nitrogen 
functional groups.
16 
Pollen typhae derived porous carbon 
prepared by KOH activation and freeze-drying yielded an in-
terconnected three-dimensional microporous framework en-
riched with oxygen functionalities, delivering a high specific 
capacitance of 437 F/g at 1 A/g and high long-term stability 
over 100,000 cycles, attributed to enhanced electrolyte acces-
sibility and defect-assisted charge storage.
38 
Rubber seed shell, 
durian shell, and palm petiole derived AC synthesized through 
eco-friendly KOH self-activation exhibited very narrow pore size 
distributions, with durian-shell-derived carbon achieving a

specific capacitance of 178 F/g due to an optimal balance 
between charge storage sites and charge transfer resistance.
39 
Peanut shell-derived AC produced by hydrothermal treatment 
followed by KOH activation showed electric double-layer ca-
pacitive behavior, with a specific capacitance of 247 F/g at 
0.25 A/g and cycling retention more than 97% after 20,000 
cycles.
40 
Furthermore, AC produced from European hornbeam 
via a rapid cavitation-assisted pyrolysis with a surface area of 
614 m
2
/g demonstrated steady electrochemical performance 
after 10,000 cycles.
41 
Surface activation of date-seed derived 
biochar with sulfuric acid revealed that controlled graphitization 
plays a critical role in electrochemical behavior, delivering a high 
specific capacitance of 487.5 F/g at 1 A/g owing to improved 
electronic conductivity and ion diffusion within ordered carbon 
domains.
42 
These investigations primarily demonstrated that 
enhanced graphitic ordering, heteroatom doping, and hierar-
chical micro-mesoporous structures improve charge storage and 
ion transport by increasing accessible surface area and electrical 
conductivity. Similar to CO
2 
adsorption, the pore structure and 
surface chemistry of AC have a significant influence on their 
electrochemical performance. Mesopores enhance electrolyte 
transport and reduce ion diffusion resistance, whilst micropores 
provide higher surface area for electric double-layer produc-
tion.
43 
Thus, to achieve high capacitance and rate capabilities, 
hierarchical micro-mesoporous structures are usually preferred. 
Beyond pristine biomass-derived carbons, heteroatom- 
engineered and hybrid systems have also been investigated to 
improve electrochemical performance. AC with optimized pore 
architectures and heteroatom functionalities achieved specific 
capacitances exceeding 200−400 F/g in aqueous electrolytes, 
emphasizing the importance of optimizing surface properties for 
high-performance supercapacitor electrodes.
44 
In another work, 
orange peel-derived AC and Ti
3
C
2
T
x 
MXene was used to 
develop a 3D porous heterostructure, with the biomass-derived 
carbon acting as an interlayer spacer to reduce MXene re-
stacking and improve electrolyte accessibility, resulting in a 
surface area of 2080 m
2
/g with a specific capacitance of 407 F/g 
at 5 mV/s and high cycling stability, demonstrating the effec-
tiveness of biomass-derived carbons in developing high- 
conductivity layered materials.
45 
These studies show that 
control over activation chemistry, pore architecture, and gra-
phitic ordering is critical to optimizing the electrochemical 
performance of biomass-derived carbons, allowing them to be 
used as low-cost, sustainable alternatives to conventional carbon 
electrodes. 
According to a recent study, biomass-derived AC has the 
potential to be tuned for dual applications in CO
2 
capture and 
electrochemical energy storage.
6 
Despite extensive research into 
biomass-derived AC materials for CO
2 
capture and electro-
chemical energy storage applications, the majority of previous 
reports focus on a single biomass precursor or application, and 
the synthesis and evaluation conditions frequently differ sig-
nificantly between studies. This makes it difficult to distinguish 
between the effects of precursor chemistry and activation pa-
rameters on porosity, surface functionality, and performance. 
Thus, this work was designed to develop a multifunctional 
material from three different underutilized industrial agro-food 
waste through a simple, scalable, and single-step synthesis under 
identical conditions, while simultaneously achieving effective 
CO
2 
adsorption and electrochemical energy storage. Further-
more, there is still a lack of understanding regarding the direct 
comparison and correlation of precursor chemistry, as well as 
the connections between synthesis conditions, pore 
architecture, surface chemistry, CO
2 
affinity, and charge-storage 
behavior in such dual-function systems. Addressing these re-
search gaps is critical for the development of sustainable ma-
terials that integrate carbon capture and energy storage into an 
integrated platform. 
Along these lines, agro-food industrial biowaste-based AC 
materials with dual functionality to act as a CO
2 
capturing 
adsorbent and electrochemical supercapacitor electrode were 
developed in this work, enabling an economical and sustainable 
material platform for such applications. AC was produced by 
upcycling three different agro-food industrial biowaste sources, 
namely flour mill waste, old corn waste, and feed waste, under 
the same synthesis conditions. The physicochemical, morpho-
logical, and textural characteristics of the produced AC materials 
were thoroughly assessed. Then, CO
2 
capture performance was 
tested in ambient conditions, and selectivity against N
2 
was 
evaluated experimentally as well as via ideal adsorbed solution 
theory (IAST) predictions. Subsequently, their electrochemical 
performance was investigated utilizing half-cell and symmetric 
full-cell experiments in 2 M KOH under different conditions, 
focusing on specific capacitance, electrical resistance, and cyclic 
performance evaluation. 
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION 
2.1. Materials 
Agthia group PJSC (Abu Dhabi) provided three types of biowaste 
materials, namely flour mill waste (BW1), old corn waste (BW2), and 
feed waste (BW3). Before KOH impregnation, the precursors were 
dried in an oven at 100 °C for 24 h, pulverized with a powder grinder, 
and sieved to obtain particles <250 μm. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 
99.99%) and N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, 99.5%) were obtained 
from Sigma-Aldrich. Air Products (UAE) supplied N
2 
and CO
2 
gases 
with purity of 99.999%. 
2.2. Synthesis of Activated Carbon 
The three biowaste samples, namely, BW1, BW2, and BW3, were used 
as starting materials to synthesize three AC materials named AC1, AC2, 
and AC3, respectively, using a single-step approach. First, a 1:3 weight 
ratio solution of biomass and KOH was prepared using 75 mL of DI 
water. To achieve homogeneous impregnation, the solution was stirred 
at room temperature for 24 h, followed by 12 h drying at 110 °C. After 
that, the samples were activated at 700 °C for 1 h with N
2 
flow. The 
samples were then thoroughly washed with DI water until the su-
pernatant achieved a neutral pH (∼7), ensuring the removal of any 
residual KOH. Finally, they were dried at 110 °C for 12 h under vacuum 
to obtain the activated carbon products. Figure 1 shows an outline of 
the synthesis process. In this investigation, all three underutilized agro-

procedure in order to provide a controlled basis for comparing their

parameters were not assumed to represent the individual optimum for 
each feedstock because they have different lignocellulosic constituents,

multivariable optimization to determine feedstock-specific optimum 
conditions.

2.5. Electrochemical Performance Evaluation 
The electrochemical half-cell performance was tested using a three- 
electrode system in 2 M KOH solution, using an electrochemical 
workstation (VMP-300, Bio-Logic). To perform this analysis, the 
working electrode was developed using the produced AC (80 wt % 
AC1, AC2, or AC3) with PVDF (10 wt %) and carbon black (10 wt %). 
First, the electrode slurries were formed by thoroughly mixing the 
components in an NMP solvent medium at ambient temperature. The 
resulting slurry was then uniformly coated over Ni foam using the drop 
casting technique, and vacuum-dried for 12 h at 80 °C. The reference 
electrode and counter electrode were Pt wire and a standard calomel 
electrode, respectively. The specific capacitance (C
s

electrode materials was determined from the measured CV profile using

Furthermore, symmetric full-cell experiments were conducted on an

were arranged face to face, with the separator in between them. 
Electrochemical characterization was performed in two-electrode mode 
using cyclic voltammetry at scan rates of 5−100 mV s
−1 
and galva-

for 1000 cycles. 
The device capacitance (C = (I*Δt)/(m*ΔV)) was determined from 
the GCD data based on the total active mass (m), where I = discharge 
current (A), Δt = discharge time, and ΔV = discharge voltage 
window (V). 
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 
3.1. Characteristics of Activated Carbon Samples 
Comparing the obtained AC yield of 23.422% for AC3 with the 
literature, they were up to 21.31%, 22.714%, and 35.5% for date 
palm seeds,
49 
poplar wood,
50 
and agroforestry waste—based 
KOH activated AC,
51 
respectively, and in the range of 31.79 to 
21.63% for AC based on steam activated eucalyptus wood 
chips.
52 
As a result, the yield obtained in this work (23.422%) is 
considered reasonable and comparable to KOH-based AC 
production, particularly given the higher burn-off typically as-
sociated with alkali activation.
